info.desc: Bat out of Hell is a 1977 album by singer Meat Loaf, songwriter Jim Steinman, and producer Todd Rundgren that became the third best-selling album worldwide behind Michael Jackson's Thriller and AC/DC's Back In Black, continuing to sell approximately 200,000 per year. Rolling Stone magazine ranked it at number 343 on its list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. Its musical style is influenced by Steinman's appreciation of Richard Wagner, Phil Spector and Bruce Springsteen. This album's title also became the title for two more Meat Loaf albums. Steinman produced the 1993 album, Bat out of Hell II: .

podcast.body: Meat Loaf's debut album, released in 1977, is a rock opera based on "Neverland," a musical adaptation of Peter Pan, featuring seven songs "oozing with teenage angst." The songs were written by Jim Steinman, who drew influences from both Wagnerian opera and rock and roll artists like Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis. Producer Todd Rundgren, a Rock and Roll Hall of Famer, ultimately funded the recording himself after discovering Meat Loaf lacked a record deal with RCA. Clive Davis, then head of CBS Records, famously rejected the project, telling Steinman he had "no idea how to write a rock song." Critic Dave Marsh of *Rolling Stone* noted Meat Loaf's "outstanding voice" but criticized his "Way Too Stage Struck" phrasing, suggesting "a little less West Side Story and a little more Bruce Springsteen." The album became one of the best-selling rock albums of all time, having sold approximately 34 million copies. "That out of hell is Meatloaf's debut album. It is a rock opera based on Neverland, which is a musical based on Peter Pan."

The album version of "Paradise by the Dashboard Light" was already not considered the greatest sounding recording. Its audio quality suffered even more significantly when the decision was made to release the song as a 7-inch single. "The version on the album isn't the greatest sounding recording, but when the decision was made to release the song as a 7-inch single, things got immeasurably worse."

podcast.body: This album was created in 1993, following the immense success of Meat Loaf's debut, despite Jim Steinman noting Meat Loaf's apprehension about creating a follow-up. It notably produced the number one single "I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)." "Steinman said that Meatloaf was afraid of having to follow that up, but they did create bat out of hell too. It was released in 1993, and it produced the number one single that you've probably heard of. I'd do anything for love, but I won't do that."
